intro: I built a small GPT-style transformer in PyTorch, trained it on Tiny Shakespeare, and then made a visualizer so I could see what was happening inside it.
orientation: This came out of the studying I was doing on my own. I could kind of explain the steps, but there were parts I still couldn't really picture.
origin: Residual connections were one of them. I knew where they went in the diagram, but I didn't have a good intuition for what they were doing. I had the same problem on the training side with backpropagation, gradient descent and Adam.

Karpathy's longer videos and 3Blue1Brown gave me a much better foundation. I followed the small GPT architecture Karpathy teaches and implemented it in PyTorch. Training it on Tiny Shakespeare kept the project small enough that I could follow the whole thing, which was what I wanted out of it.
residual: These are the lines that do the residual updates in my model. The existing values stay in x, and the attention and feed-forward parts each add an update. Once I could look at both sides of that addition, it was much easier for me to see what was happening.
visualizer: Then I had to figure out how to show the model. I wanted someone to be able to follow the values from a character all the way to the next prediction, including the parts I'd had trouble understanding myself.

None of this literally looks like the animations. I had to come up with a way to show the computation in 2D and 3D, and I wanted the scenes to use values from the model I'd trained rather than numbers I'd made up to fit the picture.
training: I also made a training view because I wanted to understand how updating the weights changes the model. That screen is a teaching illustration of gradient descent, rather than the actual shape of this model's loss surface.
takeaway: Building it helped me connect things I'd been learning separately. I can follow a character through the model now and see how it becomes a set of probabilities for what comes next.

I still find the interpretation part difficult. Being able to trace every calculation doesn't mean I can explain why the model learned a particular representation. That became more obvious as I spent time looking at the values.
